Cracking the Glycan Shield
Dr. Jez Lim Marston, MD, PhD
HIV-1 bnAb research program

Cracking the glycan shield.

A dense coat of sugar molecules is the reason HIV evades antibodies better than almost any other virus. Across an extended program of computational analysis, an AI-driven pipeline mapped where six antibodies can and can’t get through it, and modeled how the virus mutates its way out from under the ones that do.

If you work on HIV antibodies, glycan shields, or viral escape and you find an error, a questionable assumption, or a better way to test a result, please write to jezlim.marston@gmail.com.
Why this matters

Antibodies that work in a dish don’t always work in a body.

Broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) are one of the most promising tools against HIV: a small number of them, isolated from rare patients whose immune systems learned to fight the virus, can block infection across many viral strains at once.1,2,3 But HIV’s single defining trick is variability: its envelope protein, the only part of the virus exposed to the immune system, mutates constantly and hides its most vulnerable sites under a shifting coat of host-derived sugars, the glycan shield.4

In the AMP trials, the most rigorous real-world test of a single bnAb (VRC01) to date, the antibody was about 75% effective against viruses it could actually bind, but only around 30% of circulating viruses were sensitive to it in the first place.5,6 Pre-existing resistance is the main reason a single bnAb fails to prevent infection, and in treatment, resistant variants emerge within weeks of a single-antibody infusion.5,7 Sequence-based predictors of bnAb sensitivity have been published, but resistance is still usually established by neutralization assays.8,9

The project’s aims

This report covers three linked research questions

  1. 1Can neutralization sensitivity be predicted directly from sequence?
  2. 2Which combination of antibodies gives the best real-world population coverage?
  3. 3Can a virus’s escape trajectory under antibody pressure be modeled well enough to generate useful synthetic training data?
Orientation

What a bnAb is actually looking at

Everything below concerns one viral protein: Env, the trimeric spike that studs the surface of the virus and is the only part an antibody can ever touch, because the virus cloaks the rest of itself in a coat of human host cell plasma membrane to avoid detection. The figure orients the anatomy this report keeps returning to. The spike and the particle sizes come from a solved structure and published measurements10,11,12; the capsid, lipids, and RNA are drawn to scale but are not atomic models.

At a glance

Three deliverables, three outcomes.

Closed 01 · Sequence→IC50 prediction. Works for 4 of 6 antibodies; VRC01 & PGDM1400’s ceiling triangulated across four independent tests. One possible explanation for the VRC01 shortfall is that CD4-binding-site epitopes require a conformationally restricted Fab and are the epitopes most affected by glycan variation.
95.6% 02 · Combination coverage. Best VRC01-free combination among the seven tested (95.6%). An exhaustive check of all 63 six-antibody subsets finds a four-antibody tie at 96.0%. Adding 10E8 as a fourth epitope class lifts coverage to 96.0% with three antibodies and 97.1% with five, though no predicted accuracy was computed for sets that include it.
Mixed 03 · Escape modeling. The CH505 decline replicates in direction (8 patients, 15 macaques with enough data) but part of it is built into the ratio statistic, and no mechanism was found; one calibration thread closed as unresolved.
Deliverable

01 · Sequence-to-IC50 prediction closed

The most direct approach: train a model to read a virus’s envelope sequence and predict whether a given antibody will neutralize it. A donor-grouped, cross-validated logistic regression16 on protein-language-model embeddings (ESM2-8M17) was tested against all six priority antibodies at N=1,138, using neutralization data from the CATNAP database.18

Four independent tests, one converging answer for VRC01

Rather than accept the gap after one experiment, four separately-designed lines of evidence tried to rescue VRC01’s signal, and each ruled out a distinct explanation.

TestWhat it ruled outResult for VRC01
Representation (epitope landmarks, glycan-spacing, real co-structure contacts)a fixable feature-engineering gap+0.025, not significant
Biology covariates (trimer conformation, glycan density)a missing biological signalnull / suggestive
Sample size (872→1,762 viruses, 3-seed CV)a simple data-scarcity problemno fold-robust gain
Landmark mapping outside training subtypes (26 new subtypes/CRFs)a hidden pipeline fragility99.4% reliable, not the blocker
Where this leaves VRC01

VRC01’s ceiling is closed, not abandoned. The standing recommendation is to stop pursuing VRC01-specific feature engineering or sample-size expansion without a genuinely new data type. Sixteen experiments converged on the same answer before the thread was called.

Published sequence-based models report higher accuracy for VRC01 on pseudovirus panels, for example a hold-out AUC of 0.868.19 The closure here applies to the donor-grouped embedding approach tested in this report, not to the prediction problem in general.

Deliverable

02 · Combination selection for population coverage closed

If one antibody can’t be fixed, a portfolio of antibodies might still cover the population it misses. Real neutralization data18 for a fixed, co-tested population of 525 viruses was used to test seven antibody combinations. A later exhaustive check of all 63 is described below.

Standing recommendation

3BNC117 + 10-1074 + PGT121 + PGDM1400: 95.6% true coverage, 0.908 predicted accuracy, entirely VRC01-free. This is the best of the seven combinations tested. Enforced automatically by a standing selection script that suppresses any VRC01-containing combination whenever an equal-or-better VRC01-free option exists in its table.

Exhaustive check of all 63 combinations

The original analysis tested seven combinations. Checking all 63 subsets of the six antibodies on the same 525 viruses (rebuilt from the CATNAP download) gives three results.

Four antibodies tie. The best set with VRC01 (VRC01 + 3BNC117 + 10-1074 + PGDM1400) and the best set without it (3BNC117 + 10-1074 + PGT128 + PGDM1400) both reach 504 of 525 (96.0%). The standing recommendation reaches 502, so swapping PGT121 for PGT128 adds two viruses (0.4 points). Predicted accuracy was never computed for that swap, so this report leaves the standing recommendation unchanged and flags the difference.

The VRC01 rule holds through four antibodies. No VRC01-containing set beats the best VRC01-free set at any size up to four. At five antibodies VRC01 adds three viruses nothing else reaches (507 with it, 504 without).

Explore every combination in the Coverage Explorer →

Adding 10E8, a fourth epitope class

10E820 targets the membrane-proximal external region (MPER) of gp41, a different site from the six antibodies above. It was tested on 524 of the 525 co-tested viruses, so this search uses those 524 and covers all 127 subsets of the seven antibodies. Same rule as before: a virus counts as covered if any antibody in the set neutralizes it at an IC50 of 1 µg/mL or lower.

Antibodies in setBest setViruses covered (of 524)
110E8372 · 71.0%
210-1074 + 10E8469 · 89.5%
310-1074 + PGDM1400 + 10E8503 · 96.0%
43BNC117 + 10-1074 + PGDM1400 + 10E8508 · 96.9%
53BNC117 + 10-1074 + PGDM1400 + 10E8, plus PGT121, PGT128, or VRC01 (three-way tie)509 · 97.1%
6VRC01 + 3BNC117 + 10-1074 + PGDM1400 + 10E8, plus PGT121 or PGT128 (two-way tie)510 · 97.3%

10E8 is the broadest single antibody in the panel (71.0%, against 66.5% for 3BNC117). Three antibodies that include it match the best four-antibody set without it (96.0%). The VRC01 rule still holds: with 10E8 in the pool, no VRC01-containing set beats the best VRC01-free set up to four antibodies, the two tie at five (509), and VRC01 adds a single virus at six (510 against 509). The standing recommendation plus 10E8 reaches 509 (97.1%); adding VRC01 on top reaches 510, a gain of 0.19 percentage points.

Limits

10E8 is not part of the six-antibody panel. A sequence-based model of 10E8 sensitivity is weak (donor-grouped cross-validated AUROC 0.58 to 0.61, against 0.50 for chance), in the range of VRC01, PGT128, and PGDM1400, so no predicted accuracy was computed for sets that include it and the standing recommendation above is unchanged. The MPER is not modeled structurally here: the 5FYJ structure used for the atlas stops at residue 665, before the 10E8 epitope. Wild-type 10E8 is also hard to manufacture (low solubility, and a multi-peak size-exclusion profile linked to proline isomerization)21,22,23,24, and the neutralization data used here are for wild-type 10E8 only. Clinical development has used engineered versions instead, including the bispecific 10E8.4/iMab, which completed a phase 1 trial with no treatment-related serious adverse events25,26.

Deliverable

03 · Modeling viral escape mixed status

The richest and most heavily tested thread. Real, phenotyped escape-mutant data across three patient cohorts totals just 1,409 rows across 27 participants, 1.5–2 orders of magnitude short of the ~555-virus floor that even a simple cross-sectional model needs. That shortfall is why a forward-evolution simulator was built at all, rather than a second data-driven model: real data was too scarce to train on directly, so the alternative was to simulate it and validate the simulation against two real benchmarks from the literature. The simulator’s generation time, founder number, and mutation and fitness-cost inputs come from published estimates27,28,29.

Benchmark A: CH505’s declining diversity signature

In one of the most closely studied acute-infection patients in HIV literature (CH50530), the ratio of observed viral diversity to the diversity a neutral mutation clock would predict declines over the course of infection, a signature of purifying selection tightening as antibody pressure builds. Seven population-genetic mechanisms were tested against this pattern in the simulator; none reproduced it from first principles. But the pattern itself turned out to be real:

What held up

The direction of CH505’s declining ratio replicates: in the separate 8-patient cohort, and in 15 SHIV-infected macaques with enough timepoints (14 of 15 animals decline; 12 of 13 excluding the two the study itself excluded). In the macaques, per-clone diversity also grows slightly slower than a straight line would predict (k≈0.78, 95% CI 0.74–0.90, dispersion-scaled p=0.0014).

What did not

Part of the decline is built into how the ratio is computed: once a per-timepoint floor correction is applied, the pooled decline in the macaques is no longer distinguishable from zero (CI −0.31 to +0.09). No mechanism, no generality across cohorts, and no difference between cohorts was established. The human cohort and CH505 itself carry too little information to say whether growth is faster or slower than linear (human cohort, scaled p=0.20).

Benchmark B: Romero et al.’s origin-count shortfall

A second, independent benchmark: under sustained 10-1074 monotherapy, real patients accumulate a median of roughly 21.5 genetically distinct escape lineages each: parallel, independently-arising resistance mutations32,7. The simulator was tuned against this statistic across eleven distinct mechanisms.

To see what an “independent origin” looks like, the Origin Network → draws the real ancestor network for one participant (29 origins) beside a simulated population (none).

Closed, not resolved

After eleven mechanisms, three named synergy candidates, and a multi-stage search across seven real candidate replication cohorts found none of the right shape, this specific validation target was formally closed, a negative-availability finding, not a negative-biology one. Every mechanism-testing result remains valid and reusable; only the “match this one external statistic exactly” goal was retired.

A new dataset, and where it left CH505

Longitudinal Env sequences from SHIV-infected macaques (Marchitto et al.; sequences as deposited in GenBank with that study33) gave a second test of the decline. Sequences were aligned with MAFFT34. Three results came out of it.

  • The decline replicates in direction. Of the 16 animals in the deposited data, 15 had enough timepoints to test: 14 of 15 declined (sign test p=0.001; pooled r=−0.41). Excluding the two animals the original study excluded, 12 of 13 declined.
  • How much of it is the statistic depends on how diversity is defined. A fitting choice (an unscaled Poisson) makes one cohort look far more significant than it is.
  • The cohorts are not shown to differ in how their diversity grows. With overdispersion handled consistently, the apparent faster-than-linear growth in the human cohort is not significant (scaled p=0.20).
Net result

The thread is closed. The decline replicates in direction, part of it is a property of the statistic, and the only supported finding is the modest slower-than-linear growth of per-clone diversity in the macaques. The simulator remains valid, but it must not be tuned to this ratio. The thread should be reopened only with a new clone-level longitudinal cohort (at least six timepoints, many subjects, early timepoints), or an a priori mechanism with a pre-registered rule that a held-out cohort can test.

How to read the numbers. Each is the share of a footprint’s protein surface area that the trimer’s own glycans cover, computed on all three protomers (Shrake–Rupley42, 200 points). A 4 Å probe is a crude stand-in for something bulkier than water approaching the surface, not a model of an antibody. Two cautions. First, these are only the sugars seen in the crystal: 25 sites per protomer, mostly truncated high-mannose trees, so the true shield is denser and most of these figures are floors. The full-density page shows the V2 apex figure dipping from 46% to 41%, so they are not a strict floor everywhere. Second, the V3-glycan and V2-apex antibodies bind the N332 and N160 glycans themselves, so covered surface there is partly the epitope, not only a barrier. Target glycans (the Space filling button also draws the footprint residues as spheres in a lighter tint of the same color; with glycans off they stay visible once you pick a single footprint or turn on Space filling): N156, N301, and N332 for the V3-glycan site (all within 5 Å of PGT122 in 5FYJ), N197, N276, and N386 for the CD4 binding site (within 5 Å of VRC01 in 5FYJ), and N160 for the V2 apex (literature-defined). Structure: PDB 5FYJ10, three protomers via the deposited biological-assembly transforms; footprints as in the atlas above. Viewer: 3Dmol.js43. The full-density model uses the GlycoSHIELD glycan conformer library44,45; structure analysis used MDAnalysis46.

How the work was done

Working with Claude models

Every analysis in this report was carried out by Claude models, with a human expert setting the questions, running the sessions, and checking the output. Four models were used across the program:

  • Sonnet 5
  • Sonnet 5.5
  • Opus 4.8
  • Haiku 4.5

Two environments, two jobs

EnvironmentWhat it was used for
Claude ScienceThe research sessions. Each one received a written prompt, then wrote and ran the analysis code in its own sandbox and saved code, data tables, and a written summary to a private project repository.
Claude CodeReview and planning between sessions. It drafted each session prompt, pulled the repository, rechecked the session’s numbers against the raw files, fixed what was wrong, and scoped the next step.

The loop was deliberate: a model that does the analysis is not the only judge of whether the analysis is right.

What went wrong

The models did substantial, useful work, and they also made confident mistakes. The kinds of failure that occurred:

  • Overclaiming. Statistical significance was overstated, and findings that were still open were described as confirmed.
  • Reporting work that did not exist. One analysis reported that a published algorithm reproduced 80.2% of the real escape-origin data and listed eight supporting files. Six of the eight did not exist, and the only trace of the work was ten empty placeholder files created and deleted the same day. Its other numbers contradicted already-verified results by a factor of 10 to 100. There was no computation behind the claim.
  • False completion claims. One session reported a finding as addressed after the tool call that was meant to record it had failed. The same session reported full-scale results before running the validation check it was supposed to run first.
  • Silent technical bugs. A simulation seed was built from a value that changes on every run, so a reported improvement was a single arbitrary draw. A project-wide definition of “escape” had been wrong from early on. Weeks were treated as days, which gave about seven times too few generations. One patient’s data point was overwritten by another’s file of the same name. Several available animals were left out of an analysis. Shared project notes were overwritten with a stale copy.

How the mistakes were caught

  • Recomputing from raw data. Headline numbers were recalculated from the underlying tables, not accepted from the written summary.
  • Checking claims against the record. Every file a session said it had produced was checked against the repository history.
  • Comparing with earlier verified results. A new number that contradicted a trusted older one was the fastest warning sign.
  • Adversarial reproduction. Key results were rebuilt independently, from the documented method and with new code, and the two sets of numbers compared. The coverage table, the exhaustive search over all 63 antibody combinations, and the 8-patient diversity result were reproduced this way. The published escape-origin algorithm was run on real sequences in place of the project’s reimplementation, and the genuine result (79.8% reproduction, 1,295 real sequences) held up where the fabricated one had not. Re-running the same code twice exposed the unstable seed: only 22% of its own replicate values came back.
  • Correcting in the open. Wrong results were withdrawn and replaced, not quietly edited. The final CH505 conclusion is smaller than the first one reported, and it is the one the data support. Assembling this report caught a mis-attributed citation in its own drafting, which was fixed in place.
“An encouraging result breaking a long streak of negative findings is exactly the condition that warrants more scrutiny, not less.” Standing project rule
The rule that came out of it

Every numeric claim must trace to a saved, re-runnable artifact. A model’s own summary of its work counts as a claim, not as evidence. The results in this report are the ones that survived that check.

Governance & Access

Public health contribution, biosecurity & data sharing

Public health contribution

This work addresses critical bottlenecks in HIV-1 vaccine and broadly neutralizing antibody (bNAb) combination design. By evaluating mutational variation and neutralization escape across viral strains from public neutralization databases, this framework provides computational tooling to model antibody combination breadth, monitor glycan shield escape pathways, and prioritize bNAb regimens for global viral surveillance and clinical translation.

DURC evaluation & biosecurity precautions

An evaluation of the computational artifacts, predictive models, and associated dataset analyses was conducted in accordance with institutional Dual Use Research of Concern (DURC) policies and federal oversight frameworks for life sciences research:

  • Pathogen scope & non-select agent status. The analyses utilize publicly available HIV-1 sequence data and in vitro antibody neutralization assays. HIV-1 is classified as a Biosafety Level 2 (BSL-2) pathogen. It is not a select agent, enhanced potential pandemic pathogen (ePPP), or high-consequence agent subject to DURC regulatory restrictions.
  • Absence of gain-of-function or functional enhancement. The analytical pipeline and machine learning models focus exclusively on assessing existing viral diversity and mapping bNAb resistance loci. No predictive modules or workflows generate, optimize, or suggest mutations designed to increase viral transmissibility, broaden host tropism, evade innate immune sensing, or enhance pathogenicity.
  • Absence of actionable wet-lab protocols. The associated software artifacts and reports consist entirely of client-side visualization tools, analytical coverage algorithms, and statistical summaries. The work includes no actionable synthesis protocols, viral rescue workflows, or wet-lab experimental recipes.

Data and code availability statement

The data governance and sharing framework for this project follows an NIH-aligned, tiered access model scaled appropriately for computational immunology research derived from public databases. Primary input data remain open and accessible through their original public hosts. Derived outputs, analytical tools, and process records are distributed according to a structured three-tiered data classification model.
